paras: The attempted lynching of Riley Anderson was a night raid on the Greenville County jail in Greenville, South Carolina, on October 2, 1882, by a party of white and Black men seeking to hang Anderson, a Black man accused of murdering a woman and her infant. Warned in advance, Sheriff Gilreath had already hidden Anderson, and the crowd dispersed after the sheriff spoke to it. South Carolina papers carried the story chiefly from the Greenville News, dwelling on the sheriff's stratagem.

On September 26, 1882, Lou Griffin, described as a "mulatto woman," and her four-month-old child were killed in Austin Township, Greenville County, and their bodies were found the next day by white children about a mile from Dr. Crayton's farm. Several papers spelled her name Griffith and said both skulls had been crushed with a club. Her husband proved an alibi at the inquest, and the coroner's jury found that the deaths came from "strokes with a stick in the hands of Riley Anderson," a man with whom she was said to have been intimate.

Sheriff Gilreath arrested Anderson and lodged him in the Greenville jail. The Keowee Courier described him as an industrious farmer of considerable property and good character who denied any knowledge of the killings, adding that many doubted his guilt.

On the evening of Monday, October 2, a party of between 50 and 100 men, "both colored and white," gained entry to the jail by claiming to have a prisoner to deliver, according to the Greenville News as summarized by the Keowee Courier. They seized the jailer, took his keys and searched the building for Anderson, while about 150 more men waited short of the jail. Finding nothing, the band spread over the city in squads, and at 4 a.m. the search was still going on.

Anderson was not in the jail because the sheriff, having received hints of the plan that day, had talked with suspected spies in front of the building while deputies led the prisoner out the back. Two deputies kept him in the cupola of the Court House, from which he watched the procession and the search. Meanwhile the crowd moved up Main Street to a point near the Opera House and sent eight men to the sheriff's door to demand Anderson's whereabouts, which Gilreath refused to give.

Gilreath then went to the waiting crowd of about 100, told them it was his duty to protect his prisoner, and advised them to "let the law take its course." According to the Abbeville Press and Banner, the men acknowledged that they had been "outgeneraled" and scattered for their homes.

Early on Tuesday morning, October 3, Anderson was put on a train and sent to Anderson, South Carolina. No arrests of the raiders appear in the coverage, and the coverage of this raid does not report how Anderson's murder case ended.

Only white papers covered the raid, almost all of them in South Carolina, and most drew on the Greenville News. Before the raid, a Columbia wire printed in the Wheeling Register on October 2 had already called Anderson "the murderer" and attributed the killings to a quarrel with a woman he was "criminally intimate" with. The Newberry Herald gave the raid one sentence in its state-news column, while the Keowee Courier printed a longer summary describing the raiders as "well prepared and well disciplined."

Under the headline "Attempted Lynching," the Abbeville Press and Banner told the story as one of the sheriff's calm resolve, calling him "immensely popular" while still referring to Anderson as "the murderer." The Pickens Sentinel and the Weekly Union Times reported the murder and arrest but not the raid.

Counts of the crowd differ: the Newberry Herald gave about 200 men, the Greenville News summary 50 to 100 at the jail with about 150 more held back, and the Abbeville paper about 100 near the Opera House. The Newberry Herald credited the jailor with hiding Anderson, whereas the more detailed Greenville-based accounts named the sheriff and his deputies.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Riley Anderson (October 1882)
bases: An armed party raided the Greenville jail to lynch a Black prisoner accused of murder and searched the town for him, but did not find him (A5, A7, A10).

A party of 100 to 250 men acting without authority tried to seize and hang Anderson for an accused murder, but the sheriff had hidden him and no one was killed (A5, A7, A10); it was an attempted lynching.

The Newberry Herald's state-news item (A5) and the Greenville News account summarized in the Keowee Courier (A7, A11) and the Abbeville Press and Banner (A10) agree on the night raid on the jail and the failure to find Anderson, though the latter rest on the same Greenville source.

accounts.label: Greenville News (via Keowee Courier)
accounts.gist: Between 50 and 100 white and Black men entered the jail by ruse, seized the jailer and searched for Anderson while about 150 more waited; squads then searched the city, a band 'determined to lynch Anderson'.

accounts.label: Newberry Herald state news
accounts.gist: About 200 white and colored men went to the jail Monday night to lynch Anderson, but the jailor had hidden him.

accounts.label: Abbeville Press and Banner
accounts.gist: After the jail search the crowd met near the Opera House and sent a squad for the sheriff, whose speech persuaded about 100 men to go home; Anderson had been hidden in the Court House cupola and was sent by train to Anderson.

framing.detail: The Keowee Courier relayed the Greenville News account as news, calling the raiders a 'well disciplined' band without comment on their aim.
The Abbeville Press and Banner's 'Attempted Lynching' praised the sheriff's duty to the law but called Anderson 'the murderer' and described the crowd as 'jocularly' accepting defeat.
The Newberry Herald gave the raid one sentence in a state-news column.
